passages.happening:
“Then Jacob called for his sons and said, ‘Gather around so that I can tell you what will happen to you in the days to come’” (verse 1). “Come together and listen, O sons of Jacob; listen to your father Israel” (verse 2).

He begins with his firstborn. “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength, excelling in honor, excelling in power” (verse 3).

“Uncontrolled as the waters, you will no longer excel, because you went up to your father's bed, onto my couch, and defiled it” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
From here to verse 27, Jacob speaks in poetry. It is old Hebrew, full of rare words and sharp pictures. In places the meaning is uncertain, and translations differ. Two scholars, Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman, studied it in a joint thesis of 1950 (published in 1975) together with a few other poems they counted among Israel's oldest. Some read the sayings as Jacob's words handed down. Others think they took shape later, in the tribes' own history. Either way, Genesis presents them as a father's last words.

In that world a dying father's words were weighty. People believed they shaped the future of the sons who heard them. Isaac's blessing, once spoken, could not be taken back (27:33-37).

Jacob speaks to each son, and through each son to the tribe that will come from him. ‘The days to come’ means the future, the time ahead. It does not need to mean the end of the world.

Reuben comes first. He was the firstborn, with the right to lead and to inherit a double share. But ‘uncontrolled as the waters’: the Hebrew word is rare, and pictures water boiling over, reckless and unstable. Reuben slept with his father's concubine Bilhah (35:22). Then the text said only, ‘Israel heard about it.’ Now, years later, Jacob answers. Reuben loses first place.
passages.later:
The Chronicler explains: Reuben's “birthright was given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel, because Reuben defiled his father's bed” (1 Chronicles 5:1).

The Bible later reports Reuben's tribe as a small one. When Israel went to battle in Deborah's day, Reuben held back: “Why did you sit among the sheepfolds to hear the whistling for the flocks?” (Judges 5:16). Moses' blessing prays only, “Let Reuben live and not die” (Deuteronomy 33:6).
passages.asks: Reuben's one reckless act cost him the place he was born to. Ask where a moment of giving in could cost you far more than it seems to now. Then ask what self-control would protect in your life.

passages.t: Simeon and Levi: ‘Cursed be their anger’
passages.happening:
“Simeon and Levi are brothers; their swords are weapons of violence” (verse 5).

“May I never enter their council; may I never join their assembly. For they kill men in their anger, and hamstring oxen on a whim” (verse 6).

“Cursed be their anger, for it is strong, and their wrath, for it is cruel! I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This points back to chapter 34. After Shechem attacked their sister Dinah, the brothers tricked the men of the city, and Simeon and Levi killed them all. Then Jacob complained only that they had put the family in danger (34:30). Now, at the end of his life, he names what they did: violence, anger, cruelty.

To hamstring an ox is to cut the tendon at the back of its leg, so that it cannot walk. Genesis 34 says the brothers took the flocks and herds. This line adds a cruelty the earlier chapter did not tell.

Notice what Jacob curses. Not the men. Their anger. ‘Cursed be their anger.’

And the result: they will be scattered. That is what the Bible later reports for both tribes, though in very different ways.
passages.later:
Simeon's tribe did not receive its own separate land. “So the Simeonites received an inheritance within Judah's portion” (Joshua 19:9).

Levi was scattered too, but it became a blessing. When Israel worshiped the golden calf, “all the Levites gathered around him” to stand with Moses (Exodus 32:26), and Moses said, “Today you have been ordained for service to the LORD” (Exodus 32:29). The Levites became Israel's priestly tribe and were given towns all through the land: “The total number of cities you give the Levites will be forty-eight” (Numbers 35:7). The same scattering that came as judgment became a way to serve every tribe.
passages.asks: Jacob cursed his sons' anger, not his sons, and Levi's scattering later became a calling. Ask what anger in you has hurt others. Then ask whether God might turn even the consequences of your worst moments into a way to serve.

passages.happening:
“Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hand shall be on the necks of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down to you” (verse 8).

Judah is a young lion: “Like a lion he crouches and lies down; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?” (verse 9).

“The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his” (verse 10).

“He ties his donkey to the vine, his colt to the choicest branch. He washes his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes” (verse 11). “His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Judah's name sounds like the Hebrew for ‘praise’. Leah named him that: “This time I will praise the LORD” (29:35). Now Jacob says, ‘your brothers shall praise you.’

After three sons rebuked, here is the first real blessing. Judah was the son who sold Joseph (37:26-27). He was also the son who offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (44:33). Jacob gives him the leadership.

The lion is a picture of royal strength. The scepter and the staff were the signs of a king. The staff ‘between his feet’ probably pictures a ruler seated with his staff held before him.

The pictures in verses 11 and 12 are of plenty. No one would tie a donkey to a fine vine, where it would eat the grapes, unless there were so many vines it did not matter. Wine is so common he could wash his clothes in it. In early Israel, leaders rode donkeys (Judges 5:10).

The Bible later reports that Israel's lasting royal house came from Judah: King David, and the kings after him in Jerusalem.
passages.later:
The New Testament says “our Lord descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14). Revelation calls the risen Christ “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David” (Revelation 5:5). The angel promised Mary, “The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David” (Luke 1:32).

The donkey and its colt return in Zechariah: “See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). Matthew sees those words fulfilled when Jesus rode into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:5).
passages.hard:
“Until Shiloh comes” (verse 10) is one of the most debated lines in Genesis. The Hebrew is hard, and careful scholars read it in different ways. Here are the main renderings.

First, Shiloh as a name or title for a coming ruler. The Berean Standard Bible and the King James Version print it this way.

Second, ‘until he comes to whom it belongs’. This reads the Hebrew letters a little differently. The old Syriac translation takes it this way, and Ezekiel seems to echo it: “until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs” (Ezekiel 21:27).

Third, ‘until tribute comes to him’, a reading some modern translations take.

Fourth, ‘until he comes to Shiloh’, the town where Israel's tabernacle later stood. Some scholars read it this way, though no event clearly fits.

On the first three renderings, the verse looks ahead to a ruler from Judah whom the nations will obey. ‘Until’ need not mean that Judah's rule then ends. It can mark a goal: the scepter stays with Judah until it reaches the one it was meant for.

How have readers understood the king? Many Jewish readers through the centuries have read the verse as pointing to a coming king. The old Aramaic translation called Targum Onkelos, in the form that has come down to us, speaks here of the Messiah, meaning God's anointed king. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b) counts Shiloh among the names of the Messiah. Many critical scholars read the saying as celebrating the rise of King David's kingdom from Judah. Christians, from early times, have read it as finding its goal in Jesus, the son of David from the tribe of Judah, whom Revelation calls “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5).

These are readings, held in good faith. Jews and Christians still disagree about who the king is, and neither side's reading is dishonest. The second half of the verse is clear on any reading: the allegiance of the nations belongs to the ruler from Judah.

Nothing in this chapter is a prophecy about any modern nation or people.
passages.asks: The son who sold his brother received the scepter, after he offered himself for his brother. Ask whether you believe God can give a future to someone with Judah's past, including you. Then ask whose rule you are living under today.

passages.t: Zebulun to Naphtali, and a prayer
passages.happening:
“Zebulun shall dwell by the seashore and become a harbor for ships” (verse 13).

“Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the sheepfolds” (verse 14). He finds his land pleasant, “so he bent his shoulder to the burden and submitted to labor as a servant” (verse 15).

“Dan shall provide justice for his people as one of the tribes of Israel” (verse 16). “He will be a snake by the road, a viper in the path that bites the horse's heels so that its rider tumbles backward” (verse 17).

Then Jacob breaks off: “I await Your salvation, O LORD” (verse 18).

“Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will attack their heels” (verse 19). “Asher's food will be rich; he shall provide royal delicacies” (verse 20). “Naphtali is a doe set free that bears beautiful fawns” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
These sayings are short, and several play on the sons' names, as the naming stories did in chapters 29 and 30.

Dan sounds like the Hebrew for ‘judge’ or ‘provide justice’ (30:6). Gad's line is a string of words that sound like his name, meaning raid and raiders. Asher means ‘happy’ (30:13), and he gets rich food. Issachar's name was linked with wages (30:18). Here he trades his freedom for a comfortable place, and ends up a laborer.

Zebulun ‘by the seashore’ is hard to match with the land Joshua later gave it, which lay inland in Galilee (Joshua 19:10-16). Many readers take the line to mean that Zebulun would reach the coast and its trade, not that its border touched the sea.

Naphtali's line is uncertain. The Berean Standard Bible reads ‘beautiful fawns’. The same Hebrew can be read as ‘beautiful words’, as in the King James Version.

In the middle of all this, the only time the LORD is named in the poem, Jacob prays. ‘I await Your salvation, O LORD.’ After the dark sayings about Dan and his snake, the dying man lifts his eyes. Salvation means rescue, deliverance. Jacob's hope is not in his sons. It is in God.
passages.later:
The Bible later reports that Dan's tribe could not hold its first land: “The Amorites forced the Danites into the hill country” (Judges 1:34). They moved to the far north and took a city there: “They named it Dan, after their forefather Dan” (Judges 18:29). Samson, one of Israel's judges, came “from the clan of the Danites” (Judges 13:2).

Old Simeon, holding the baby Jesus in the temple, spoke words close to Jacob's prayer: “For my eyes have seen Your salvation” (Luke 2:30).
passages.asks: In the middle of hard words about his sons, Jacob stopped and prayed, ‘I await Your salvation, O LORD.’ Ask what you are worried about for the people you love. Then ask whether you have stopped, in the middle of that worry, to look to God.

passages.happening:
Jacob turns to Joseph: “a fruitful vine by a spring, whose branches scale the wall” (verse 22).

“The archers attacked him with bitterness; they aimed at him in hostility. Yet he steadied his bow, and his strong arms were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, in the name of the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel” (verses 23-24).

God will bless him “with blessings of the heavens above, with blessings of the depths below, with blessings of the breasts and womb” (verse 25). “May they rest on the head of Joseph, on the brow of the prince of his brothers” (verse 26).

Last comes Benjamin. “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours the prey, in the evening he divides the plunder” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Joseph's saying is the longest with Judah's. The two sons will lead Israel: Judah in the south, Joseph's tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, in the north.

The Hebrew word for ‘fruitful’ sounds like Ephraim, the name Joseph gave his son because God made him fruitful (41:52). The picture is of a vine so full of life that it climbs over the wall. Older versions read ‘a fruitful bough’; the sense is the same.

‘The archers’ are not named. Many readers think of all who attacked Joseph: his brothers, Potiphar's wife, the years of prison. He did not break. His arms were made strong by God.

Listen to the names Jacob piles up for God: the Mighty One of Jacob, the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel, the God of your father, the Almighty. A rock is a place of safety that does not move. ‘Blessing’ comes again and again: of rain from above, of springs from below, of children.

‘Prince of his brothers’ translates a word that means one set apart. The boy his brothers threw out is set apart among them.

Benjamin, the youngest, the one everyone protected, is a fierce wolf. The Bible later reports a tribe of fighters.
passages.later:
Moses' blessing echoes Jacob's for Joseph: “May his land be blessed by the LORD with the precious dew from heaven above and the deep waters that lie beneath” (Deuteronomy 33:13). A psalm sings, “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psalm 18:2).

From Benjamin's tribe came the judge Ehud, “a left-handed Benjamite” (Judges 3:15), and Israel's first king, Saul, son of “a Benjamite, a powerful man” (1 Samuel 9:1). The apostle Paul was “of the tribe of Benjamin” (Philippians 3:5).
passages.asks: Joseph was shot at by many archers and his arms were made strong by the Mighty One of Jacob. Ask what has been aimed at you. Then ask where you have found, or could find, the strength that does not come from yourself.

passages.happening:
“These are the tribes of Israel, twelve in all, and this was what their father said to them. He blessed them, and he blessed each one with a suitable blessing” (verse 28).

Then Jacob gives his last instruction. “I am about to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite” (verse 29). It is the cave of Machpelah near Mamre, which Abraham bought (verse 30). “There Abraham and his wife Sarah are buried, there Isaac and his wife Rebekah are buried, and there I buried Leah” (verse 31).

“When Jacob had finished instructing his sons, he pulled his feet into the bed and breathed his last, and he was gathered to his people” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
Here, for the first time, the narrator counts Jacob's sons as ‘the tribes of Israel, twelve in all’. Twelve brothers have become the start of a nation.

The narrator calls it all a blessing, even the hard words to Reuben, Simeon and Levi. Each son received what was ‘suitable’ for him. A true word, even a hard one, can be a gift.

Jacob's burial charge repeats the details of Abraham's purchase like someone reading from the deed: the field, the cave, Ephron the Hittite, Mamre (chapter 23). The family's only land in Canaan is a grave. Jacob wants to lie in it, with the promise.

Notice who is named: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah. Not Rachel, who lies by the road to Bethlehem. Leah, the wife who was not loved as Rachel was, rests beside Jacob in the end.

‘Gathered to his people’ was the Hebrew way of speaking of death as joining those who had gone before. Jacob is gathered to his people the moment he dies in Egypt, long before his body reaches the cave. So the phrase seems to mean more than burial.

He pulls his feet up into the bed and dies, quietly, in peace, with his sons around him, as God promised at Beersheba (46:4).
passages.later:
The same words were used of Abraham: he “breathed his last and died, old and contented, and was gathered to his people” (Genesis 25:8).

The twelve tribes run through the whole Bible, to its last book, where John hears the tribes named again: “From the tribe of Judah 12,000 were sealed, from the tribe of Reuben 12,000” (Revelation 7:5).
passages.asks: Jacob died with his last words spoken and his burial planned in the land of promise. Ask whether there are words you need to say to the people you love while you still can. Then ask where your hope will rest when your own time comes.
